docs.title: Orion
docs.text:
Orion is a cluster manager for PostgreSQL. It runs PostgreSQL clusters with a primary and one or more standbys, fails over automatically when the primary fails, and makes sure clients only connect to the current primary. You can run Orion on virtual machines and on Kubernetes.

Orion is a fork of stolon. It keeps stolon's keeper, sentinel and proxy, and adds a REST api with a cli on top of it, secured with TLS and client certificates.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
Component Binary What it does keeper orion-keeper Manages one PostgreSQL instance and converges it to the cluster view of the leader sentinel. sentinel orion-sentinel Discovers and monitors the keepers and proxies, and computes the optimal cluster view. proxy orion-proxy The access point for clients. It only forwards connections to the current primary, and closes connections to old primaries. api orion-api Manages Orion clusters with a REST api, with TLS and client certificates (mTLS). cli orion-cli Consumes the api.

All components keep their state in a highly available store (etcd, consul or the Kubernetes api server), so they can run anywhere, come and go, and change their addresses.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• API certificates: the certificates the api and the cli use, and how to create them.
  • Bootstrap design: the design of TLS and the bootstrap of the api.

Note

The rest of the documentation still comes from stolon and describes stolon's behaviour. Until it is reviewed and updated for Orion, it lives in docs/stolon in the repository.

docs.title: TLS and bootstrap design
docs.text: This page describes how Orion secures the connections between its components with TLS, and how the api and the cli get their certificates. Most of it is not implemented yet: see Roadmap for what is done and what is planned.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• All connections use TLS, and clients log in with a client certificate (mTLS). There is no plain HTTP api, and no bearer token.
  • Orion has its own CA: a root, one intermediate for all server certificates, and a separate client intermediate per service (api, PostgreSQL, etcd, RustFS, ...).
  • The private keys of the root and the intermediates live with the cli, encrypted, and never stay next to the api.
  • You can start the api without any certificates. It then starts in bootstrap mode: the cli connects with a shared secret, gets all certificates, and the api switches to normal mode with mTLS.
  • You can also bring your own certificates (e.g. created with orion-cli pki init, or mounted from Kubernetes Secrets). The api then never sees a CA key.
# Generate the CA, the intermediates, the api server certificate and the cli client certificate
orion-cli pki init --host orion-api.example.com

# Copy ~/.orion/api to the api host, and start the api with it
orion-api --pki-dir ~/.orion/api

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Zero configuration: the api can start without any certificates and create everything it needs.
  • Server and client certificates for everything: the api, the cli, PostgreSQL, etcd, RustFS and the other Orion components all use TLS, with server certificates for the servers and client certificates for the clients.
  • CA keys away from the api: the api is the component that is exposed the most. The private keys of the root and the intermediates are with the cli, encrypted with a passphrase. New certificates and renewals go through the cli.
  • The cli and the api manage the certificates: no external tooling is needed (but you can use it, see Bring your own PKI).

docs.title: The PKI
docs.text:
Root CA (5y)
├── Server intermediate (3y)
│   ├── api server certificate (1y)          CN=orion-api
│   ├── PostgreSQL server certificates       (later)
│   ├── etcd server certificates             (later)
│   └── RustFS server certificates           (later)
├── api client intermediate (3y)
│   └── cli client certificate (1y)          CN=orion-cli
├── PostgreSQL client intermediate           (later)
├── etcd client intermediate                 (later)
└── RustFS client intermediate               (later)
  • All server certificates can share the server intermediate.
  • Client certificates get a separate intermediate per service. A server trusts only the client intermediate of its own service, so a client certificate for etcd can't be used to log in to the api, or to PostgreSQL.
  • The CN of a client certificate is the identity of the client (e.g. orion-cli).

docs.title: Validity
docs.text:
Certificate Validity Root CA 5 years Intermediates 3 years Server and client certificates 1 year
  • A certificate never outlives its parent: its expiry is capped at the expiry of the certificate that signs it.
  • The start of the validity (NotBefore) is 5 minutes in the past, so hosts with a slightly late clock accept a new certificate.
  • All validities can be configured (e.g. orion-cli pki init --root-validity 5y --leaf-validity 1y).
  • The api logs a warning when its certificate, or a certificate in its chain, expires within 30 days.

The root is valid for 5 years instead of the usual 10, which leaves time to move to post-quantum signatures (see Cryptography). Shorter lifetimes for the server and client certificates may follow, together with automatic renewal.

docs.title: Names on the api certificate
docs.text:
A client only accepts a server certificate if the name it connects to is on it, as a Subject Alternative Name (SAN). The api certificate always gets localhost, 127.0.0.1 and ::1, plus:

How the certificate is made Detected names Extra names orion-cli pki init The api host of the cli (--host) --api-san (repeatable) Bootstrap mode The hostname and IP addresses of the api host, and the host of --base-url Sent by the cli

In most cases the detected names are enough; the extra names are for load balancers, DNS aliases or Kubernetes Service names (orion-api.<namespace>.svc, ...).

docs.title: Ports and modes
docs.text:
Port Protocol Bootstrap mode Normal mode api (--port, default 8443) TLS Temporary self-signed certificate, no client certificate, only the bootstrap endpoints (protected with HMAC) Server certificate from the PKI, client certificate required, the normal api probe (--probe-port, default 8080) HTTP /livez, /readyz, /status reports bootstrap /livez, /readyz, /metrics, /status reports normal

The api port has one mode at a time:

  • In normal mode, the api port requires a valid client certificate during the TLS handshake (RequireAndVerifyClientCert). There are no exceptions: a connection without a valid client certificate never reaches an api handler.
  • When the api switches from bootstrap mode to normal mode, it stops the bootstrap server, which closes all its connections, and starts the normal server on the same port. A bootstrap connection (without a client certificate) can't stay open into normal mode.

The probe port has no TLS and no authentication, and it serves nothing sensitive:

Endpoint Returns /livez 200 when the process is alive (liveness; it doesn't check the store). /readyz 200 when the api port serves, in either mode, isn't shutting down and the store answers; 503 otherwise. In bootstrap mode the api must be ready too, or Kubernetes doesn't route the bootstrap traffic to it. /status The mode, e.g. {"mode":"bootstrap"} or {"mode":"normal"}. The cli checks it before it bootstraps. /metrics Prometheus metrics, e.g. the expiry of the certificates.

docs.title: Bootstrap
docs.text: When the api starts without certificates, it starts in bootstrap mode.

docs.title: The shared secret
docs.text:
The api and the cli prove to each other that they know a shared secret.

  • Give the secret to the api in an environment variable or a file, not as a command-line argument (arguments are visible in ps).
  • Without a secret, the api generates one (at least 128 bits) and logs it once.
  • A secret you choose yourself must have a minimum length: with an active man in the middle, a weak secret can be guessed offline.
  • The secret can be used once, expires (e.g. after 24 hours), and failed attempts are rate limited.

docs.title: The flow
docs.text:
cli                                                    api (bootstrap mode)
 |                                                      |
 |-- GET /status (probe port) ------------------------->|
 |<-------------------------------- {"mode":"bootstrap"}|
 |                                                      |
 |== TLS (self-signed api certificate) ================>|
 |<-- challenge (api nonce) ----------------------------|
 |-- HMAC(secret, api nonce, TLS exporter), cli nonce ->|
 |<-------------- HMAC(secret, cli nonce, TLS exporter)-|
 |                                                      |
 |-- cli public key, extra SANs ----------------------->|  generate root, intermediates,
 |                                                      |  api and cli certificates
 |<-- archive ------------------------------------------|
 |-- stored -------------------------------------------->|
 |                                                      |  switch to normal mode
 |== mTLS (cli client certificate) ====================>|
 |-- confirm ------------------------------------------>|  delete CA keys and archive
 |<-- ok -----------------------------------------------|
  1. The cli checks on the probe port that the api is in bootstrap mode.
  2. The cli generates its key pair in ~/.orion/cli/, with the private key encrypted with a passphrase.
  3. The cli connects to the api port. The api has a temporary self-signed certificate, so the cli can't verify it.
  4. The api and the cli prove to each other that they know the secret, with HMAC. The HMAC also covers keying material exported from the TLS session (ConnectionState.ExportKeyingMaterial, see RFC 9266). The secret itself is never sent.
  5. The cli sends its public key, and optionally extra names for the api certificate.
  6. The api generates the root, the intermediates, its own server certificate and the cli client certificate, and sends the archive:
  7. all certificates and chains, as they are (they are public);
  8. the private key of the cli certificate and the private keys of the root and the intermediates, encrypted with the public key of the cli.
  9. The cli stores the archive and reports stored.
  10. The api switches to normal mode, but keeps the CA keys.
  11. The cli connects again, now with mTLS and its new client certificate, and confirms. This proves that its certificate works. The confirmation can be repeated.
  12. The api deletes the CA keys and the archive.

After the bootstrap, the api has only its own server certificate and key, and the chains to verify clients. It can't issue or renew any certificate by itself; that goes through the cli.

docs.title: Why this is safe
docs.text:
• A man in the middle can't take over the bootstrap. The api certificate is self-signed, so the cli can't verify it, and a man in the middle could set up a TLS session with each side. But the HMAC covers keying material of the TLS session, which differs between the two sessions, so he can't forward the proofs. And he never sees the secret.
  • The api proves itself too. Both sides prove that they know the secret, so the cli knows it talks to the real api. It doesn't need to pin a CA fingerprint.
  • The CA keys are encrypted to the cli. Only the holder of the private key of the cli can read them, also when the archive is intercepted or recorded.
  • The api deletes the CA keys as soon as the cli has proven that it can use its certificate.

docs.title: State and recovery
docs.text:
The api stores the state of the bootstrap, so it can continue after a restart:

State api port CA keys on the api bootstrapping Bootstrap mode Not yet, or generated but not handed over handed-over Normal mode Yes, until the cli confirms confirmed Normal mode No
  • After a restart, the api continues in the state it was in. The secret stays valid until it expires, and a CA that was already generated is reused.
  • If the cli never confirms (e.g. it lost the archive), nobody can connect to the api. Restart the api with --rebootstrap to start over. The api doesn't fall back to bootstrap mode by itself.

docs.title: Bring your own PKI
docs.text:
When you give the api a certificate, a key and a CA (--tls-cert-file, --tls-key-file and --tls-ca-file), it uses them and generates nothing: there is no bootstrap mode, and the api never has a CA key.

Use it to:

  • create the certificates with the cli, so the CA keys never touch the api host:
orion-cli pki init --host orion-api.example.com
  • run the api on Kubernetes, with the certificates (created by the cli) mounted from Secrets;
  • use certificates from your own PKI (e.g. cert-manager or Vault).

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
• In normal mode, the api port requires a client certificate signed by the api client intermediate.
  • The api puts the identity of the client (the CN of its certificate) in the request context. The authentication is a chain of authenticators that all return the same identity (a name and groups), so other methods can be added without changing the handlers.
  • The --token flag is removed (it was never checked), and so is --tls=false: TLS is always on.

OIDC/OAuth can be added later as another authenticator, for people who log in with an identity provider (Keycloak, Entra ID, Okta, ...): the api checks JWT bearer tokens, and the cli logs in with the device flow. OIDC tokens come without a client certificate, so the api port then verifies a client certificate only when it is given, and a middleware requires either a certificate or a token.

docs.title: Cryptography
docs.text:
What Algorithm Quantum safe Certificate keys and signatures ECDSA P-256, keys in PKCS#8 (configurable, e.g. RSA) ❌ Key pair of the cli, encryption of the archive HPKE with ML-KEM-768 + X25519 (crypto/hpke, MLKEM768X25519) ✅ Private key of the cli on disk Passphrase → scrypt or Argon2id → AES-256-GCM ✅ TLS key exchange The Go default: X25519MLKEM768 and SecP256r1MLKEM768 ✅ (Go clients and servers) HMAC in the bootstrap HMAC-SHA256 ✅
  • Encryption must be quantum safe now: an attacker can record the archive today and decrypt it when quantum computers exist ("harvest now, decrypt later"), and the archive holds the CA keys. The hybrid HPKE is safe as long as either ML-KEM or X25519 holds, and it is in the Go standard library.
  • Signatures only need to hold while a certificate is valid, and they can't be broken afterwards. Go has no ML-DSA (FIPS 204) in crypto/x509 yet, and most clients (libpq, JDBC, ...) can't use ML-DSA certificates. Orion uses ECDSA P-256 for now and moves to ML-DSA when Go and the clients support it.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
Where Directory Contents api ~/.orion/api/ (--pki-dir) Its server certificate and key, the chains to verify clients, and during the bootstrap the bootstrap state and the archive cli ~/.orion/cli/ Its key pair, its client certificate, the chains, and the encrypted CA keys

The directories are only readable for their owner, and private keys are stored with mode 0600.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
Implemented in the first PR:

  • The PKI library (pkg/tls): root, server intermediate, client intermediate, server and client certificates, ECDSA P-256, validity rules.
  • orion-cli pki init: generates the CA, the intermediates, the api server certificate and the cli client certificate.
  • The api with your own certificates: mTLS on the api port, the identity of the client in the request context.
  • The probe port with /livez, /readyz and /status (Kubernetes conventions; graceful shutdown on SIGTERM).
  • The cli connects to the api with mTLS.
  • /metrics on the probe port, with the expiry of the certificates.

Later, each in its own PR:

  • Encrypt the CA keys on the cli with a passphrase. For now, orion-cli pki init stores them unencrypted, readable for the owner only.
  • Bootstrap mode, with the shared secret, the HMAC, the archive, the confirmation and --rebootstrap.
  • Certificate management in the cli and the api (issue, renew, list), and automatic renewal.
  • Server and client certificates for PostgreSQL, etcd, RustFS and the other components.
  • Several api instances (HA), with the bootstrap state in shared storage and a lock.
  • Kubernetes: certificates created by the cli, mounted from Secrets.
  • OIDC/OAuth authentication.
  • ML-DSA signatures, when Go and the clients support them.

docs.title: Alternatives that were not chosen
docs.text: Alternative Why not Bootstrap on the api, copy the certificates to the cli with ssh Needs ssh access and manual steps. Pin the fingerprint of the CA in the cli (like kubeadm join) The shared secret also authenticates the api, so it is not needed. Prove the cli key with an encrypted nonce The shared secret replaces it. Write the cli key pair on the api host when no cli key is given The CA keys would be next to the key that decrypts them. A local cli bootstraps over localhost instead. A separate bootstrap port One api port with two modes is simpler, and a connection can't move from one mode to the other. One port with a middleware that allows some endpoints without a client certificate The TLS handshake can enforce mTLS by itself; the health endpoints are on the probe port. Fall back to bootstrap mode automatically when the cli doesn't confirm Hard to predict; --rebootstrap is explicit. RSA or Ed25519 for the certificates RSA is slow and large; Ed25519 is not supported by all PostgreSQL clients.

docs.title: Certificates for the api and the cli
docs.text: The Orion api only accepts TLS connections with a client certificate (mTLS). This page describes how to create the certificates with orion-cli pki init, and how to run the api and the cli with them. For the design behind it, see TLS and bootstrap design.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
On the machine where you run the cli:

orion-cli pki init --host orion-api.example.com

Copy ~/.orion/api to the api host (e.g. to /etc/orion/api), and start the api:

orion-api --pki-dir /etc/orion/api --cluster-name mycluster --store-backend etcdv3

Check the connection from the cli:

orion-cli --host orion-api.example.com connect
# Connected to the api as orion-cli (client-certificate)

docs.title: What orion-cli pki init creates
docs.text:
Root CA
├── server intermediate
│   └── orion-api      (server certificate of the api)
└── api-clients intermediate
    └── orion-cli      (client certificate of the cli)
Directory File Contents ~/.orion/api (--api-dir) server.crt The server certificate of the api, followed by the server intermediate server.key The private key of the server certificate client-ca.crt The api-clients intermediate: the api only accepts client certificates signed by it ~/.orion/cli (--pki-dir) tls.crt, tls.key The client certificate of the cli, and its private key ca.crt The root, to verify the api ca/ The certificates and private keys of the root and the intermediates
  • Private keys are only readable for their owner (mode 0600).
  • The api directory has no CA key. Keep ~/.orion/cli/ca safe: whoever has it can create certificates that the api accepts. For now the CA keys are stored unencrypted; encryption with a passphrase is planned.
  • orion-cli pki init doesn't overwrite existing files, unless you add --force.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Default Description --host, -H The configured api host Added to the api certificate. --api-san Extra names or IP addresses for the api certificate (can be repeated), e.g. a load balancer or a Kubernetes Service name. --api-dir ~/.orion/api Where the api files are stored. --pki-dir ~/.orion/cli Where the cli files are stored. --key-algorithm ecdsa-p256 ecdsa-p256, rsa-2048, rsa-3072 or rsa-4096. --root-validity 5y Validity of the root. Accepts years (y), days (d) and Go durations (e.g. 8760h). --intermediate-validity 3y Validity of the intermediates. --leaf-validity 1y Validity of the api and cli certificates. --force Overwrite existing files.

The api certificate is always valid for localhost, 127.0.0.1 and ::1.

docs.title: Running the api
docs.text:
Option Environment variable Default Description --port ORIONAPI_PORT 8443 The api: TLS, a client certificate is required. --probe-port ORIONAPI_PROBE_PORT 8080 /livez, /readyz, /status and /metrics: plain HTTP, no authentication. --shutdown-delay ORIONAPI_SHUTDOWN_DELAY 5s On SIGTERM, the time /readyz returns 503 before the api stops. --pki-dir ORIONAPI_PKI_DIR ~/.orion/api The directory with server.crt, server.key and client-ca.crt. --tls-cert-file ORIONAPI_TLS_CERT_FILE <pki-dir>/server.crt Use another file for the server certificate. --tls-key-file ORIONAPI_TLS_KEY_FILE <pki-dir>/server.key Use another file for the private key. --tls-ca-file ORIONAPI_TLS_CA_FILE <pki-dir>/client-ca.crt Use another file for the CA of the client certificates.
  • The api doesn't start without its certificates. Starting without certificates (bootstrap mode) is planned.
  • The api reads its certificates at start. After you replace them (e.g. after a renewal), restart the api.
  • At start, and once a day, the api logs a warning for every certificate it loaded that expires within 30 days.
  • The api container image reads its certificates from /etc/orion/api (ORIONAPI_PKI_DIR). Mount them there, e.g. from a Kubernetes Secret, and make sure the orion user can read the private key.

docs.title: Probe port
Metrics
docs.text:
/metrics on the probe port returns the metrics of the api in the Prometheus format. The api doesn't use --metrics-listen-address, which the other components use for their metrics.

Metric Type Labels Description orion_api_certificate_expiry_timestamp_seconds gauge common_name, serial, ca Expiry of each certificate the api loaded at start (its certificate, its chain and the CA of the clients), in seconds since the unix epoch. orion_api_requests_total counter method, route, code Requests on the api port, after authentication. route is the path of the route, e.g. /v1/cluster/keepers/{id}. orion_api_request_duration_seconds histogram method, route Duration of those requests. orion_cluster_identifier gauge cluster_name, component Always 1, with component="api". The other components have it too.

The api also serves the standard Go and process metrics (go_*, process_*).

To alert on certificates that expire within 30 days:

- alert: OrionAPICertificateExpiresSoon
  expr: orion_api_certificate_expiry_timestamp_seconds - time() < 30 * 24 * 3600
  labels:
    severity: warning
  annotations:
    summary: "Certificate {{ $labels.common_name }} of the orion api expires within 30 days"

Because the api reads its certificates at start, the metric shows the certificates it uses, not the files on disk. After you renew the certificates and restart the api, the alert clears.

docs.title: Using the cli
docs.text:
All cli commands that talk to the api log in with the client certificate in --pki-dir (default ~/.orion/cli). orion-cli connect checks the connection: it calls /v1/whoami, which returns the identity the api sees.

You can also use another client, e.g. curl:

curl --cacert ~/.orion/cli/ca.crt --cert ~/.orion/cli/tls.crt --key ~/.orion/cli/tls.key \
  https://orion-api.example.com:8443/v1/whoami

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Error Cause certificates not found (api) The files are not in --pki-dir. Run orion-cli pki init, and copy the api files. client certificate not found (cli) The files are not in the --pki-dir of the cli. Run orion-cli pki init. certificate signed by unknown authority The cli and the api use certificates of different CAs. Copy the api files of the same pki init to the api. certificate is valid for ..., not ... The name you connect to is not on the api certificate. Add it with --api-san, and run pki init --force. tls: certificate required (client) The client didn't send a client certificate.
